# ctsem

<!-- badges: start -->
[![R-CMD-check](https://github.com/cdriveraus/ctsem/workflows/R-CMD-check/badge.svg)](https://github.com/cdriveraus/ctsem/actions)
[![CRAN status](https://www.r-pkg.org/badges/version/ctsem)](https://cran.r-project.org/package=ctsem)
[![Downloads](https://cranlogs.r-pkg.org/badges/grand-total/ctsem)](https://cran.r-project.org/package=ctsem)
<!-- badges: end -->

ctsem fits continuous and discrete time dynamic models to longitudinal data in
R: panel data, intensive longitudinal data or a single time series.
Observations can be at any times, and the times can differ between subjects.

[Website](https://cdriveraus.github.io/ctsem/) ·
[Getting started](https://cdriveraus.github.io/ctsem/articles/ctsem.html) ·
[New in version 4](NEW-IN-4.md) ·
[Tutorial paper](https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv/4q9ex_v3)

## Features

- Multiple interacting processes, including higher order (such as oscillating)
  and nonlinear dynamics.
- Effects of time-varying inputs, such as interventions.
- Multiple indicators, which can be continuous, binary, ordinal, counts or
  censored.
- Individual differences in any parameter, including at multiple nested levels
  (such as people within couples).
- Covariate effects on any parameter.
- Maximum likelihood, or Bayesian estimation by optimisation or sampling.
- Tools for testing a model's fit and finding how to improve it.
- Latent growth curve, latent change score and cross-lagged panel models as
  special cases.

Version 4 adds an estimation engine written in Julia, now the default. It is two
to three times faster than the Stan backend, uses multiple cores, and needs no
compilation for new models. Random effects are integrated with a Laplace
approximation, which estimates individual differences in the dynamics more
accurately than earlier versions did.

## Installation

```r
remotes::install_github('cdriveraus/ctsem')
library(ctsem)
ctJuliaInstall()   # once, to set up Julia
```

The first fit after installing takes a few minutes longer while the engine
compiles. Without Julia, `ctFit(..., backend = 'stan')` fits models as ctsem 3
did.

<details><summary>Compiler problems on Windows</summary>

Installing from GitHub compiles the package, which on Windows needs the Rtools
version that matches your R. If compiling fails, check that
`rstan` itself works, and try adding this line to `~/.R/Makevars.win`:

```
CXX17FLAGS += -mtune=native -Wno-ignored-attributes -Wno-deprecated-declarations
```

The [Stan forums](https://discourse.mc-stan.org/) cover other compiler
problems.

</details>

## Example

Milk yield and fat percentage of 53 cows, recorded on most days of a lactation,
from the [doBy](https://cran.r-project.org/package=doBy) package. ctsem takes
data in long format: one row per cow and occasion, with columns for the id, the
time and each measured variable. Missing values are `NA`, and the times can be
irregular and differ between subjects.

```{r firstmodel, results = 'hide'}
library(ctsem)
data(milkman_rdm1, package = 'doBy')

milk <- data.frame(
  cow   = milkman_rdm1$cowno,
  day   = milkman_rdm1$dfc,                     # days since calving
  yield = as.numeric(scale(milkman_rdm1$my)),
  fat   = as.numeric(scale(milkman_rdm1$fatpct)))

model <- ctModel(
  type = 'ct',                        # 'dt' for discrete time
  LAMBDA = diag(2),                   # two processes, one indicator each
  manifestNames = c('yield', 'fat'),
  latentNames = c('yield', 'fat'),
  time = 'day',
  id = 'cow')

fit <- ctFit(milk, model)
```

Anything not given to `ctModel()` takes a default. Here the two processes can
affect each other, and each cow has its own average levels and starting values.

```{r firstsummary}
summary(fit)$popmeans
```

The `drift` parameters are rates of change per day, the time unit of the data.
`drift_yield` and `drift_fat` are the auto effects, and `drift_yield_fat` is
the effect of fat on the rate of change of yield, `drift_fat_yield` the
reverse. The `diff` parameters describe the random shocks to the processes,
`mvar` the measurement error, `mm` the average levels of the measurements and
`T0m` the starting values. `diff_fat_yield` is a parameter for the correlation
of the shocks, which `summary(fit)$parmatrices` reports as `DIFFUSIONcor`.
`summary(fit)$popsd` gives how much the cows differ.

Whether the processes return to equilibrium after a disturbance, and how
quickly, depends on the whole drift matrix. They do when every eigenvalue of the
matrix has a negative real part:

```{r firsteigen}
drift <- ctSummaryMatrices(fit)$estimate$DRIFT
eigen(drift)$values
log(2) / abs(eigen(drift)$values)    # half-lives in days
```

```{r firsthalflives, include = FALSE}
halflives <- round(sort(log(2) / abs(eigen(drift)$values)))
```

A disturbance halves in about `r halflives[1]` days along one combination of
the processes and `r halflives[2]` days along the other. That is slower than
either auto effect alone would give, because the cross effects form a loop:
higher fat lowers yield, and lower yield raises fat.

```{r firstdiscrete, fig.height = 4.4, fig.width = 8, fig.alt = "Auto and cross regression coefficients plotted against time intervals of up to 150 days. The autoregressions fall towards zero, and the effect of fat on yield becomes negative, is strongest at about six weeks, and then returns towards zero; the effect of yield on fat stays near zero."}
ctDiscretePars(fit, times = seq(0, 150, by = 1), plot = TRUE)
```

The same effects as regression coefficients, as they change with the time
interval. A higher fat percentage is followed by a lower yield, most strongly
after about six weeks, and yield has little effect on fat. The
[dynamics vignette](https://cdriveraus.github.io/ctsem/articles/dynamics.html)
explains how to read these.

```{r firstplot, fig.height = 4.4, fig.width = 8, fig.alt = "Observed yield and fat percentage for two cows over one lactation, with the model's expected trajectory and uncertainty band tracking each series."}
ctPredict(fit, subjects = unique(milk$cow)[1:2], plot = TRUE)
```

Observations for two cows, with the model's predictions and their uncertainty.

## Covariate effects

This example estimates the effect of diet on the growth of chicks
(`ChickWeight`, in base R):

```{r chickdata}
chickdata <- ChickWeight
chickdata <- cbind(chickdata, model.matrix(~ Diet - 1, chickdata))  # dummy code diet
colnames(chickdata)[5:8] <- paste0('Diet_', 1:4)
chickdata$weight <- scale(chickdata$weight)
```

```{r chickmodel, results = 'hide'}
m <- ctModel(
  type = 'ct',
  LAMBDA = diag(1),
  manifestNames = 'weight',
  latentNames = 'Lweight',
  time = 'Time',
  id = 'Chick',
  DRIFT = 'a11, transform=param',                   # allow growth (no sign restriction)
  MANIFESTMEANS = 0,                                # fix the measurement intercept...
  CINT = 'cint, tipreds=c(Diet_2,Diet_3,Diet_4)',   # ...and estimate the process intercept
  TIpredNames = paste0('Diet_', 2:4),               # diet 1 is the baseline
  tipredDefault = FALSE)                            # no other covariate effects

f <- ctFit(chickdata, m, priors = TRUE)
```

In `ctModel()`, a string is a free parameter and a number a fixed value. Options
follow the parameter's name, such as `tipreds` for covariate effects or
`indvarying` for random effects; `ctPar()` writes these strings.

The same models can be written in lavaan, Mplus or brms style syntax with
`ctModelLavaan()`, `ctModelMplus()` and `ctModelFormula()`, see the
[model syntax vignette](https://cdriveraus.github.io/ctsem/articles/model-syntax.html).

```{r chickestimates}
summary(f)$popmeans[c('a11', 'cint'), ]
summary(f)$tipreds
```

The rate at which a chick's weight changes is `a11` times its current weight,
plus `cint`. `a11` is positive, so the heavier a chick, the
faster it grows. `cint` is the growth rate for diet 1 at the average weight. It
varies between chicks, as a free intercept does by default, and the diets
shift it. Diets 3 and 4 raise the growth rate at any weight, compared with
diet 1, and because heavier chicks grow faster, the difference compounds over
time. The effect of diet 2 is smaller and its interval includes zero.

```{r chickpredict, fig.height = 4.2, fig.width = 8, fig.alt = "Predicted weight trajectories for one chick from each of the four diets, based on the diet covariates alone, separating into four increasing curves."}
ctPredict(f, plot = TRUE, removeObs = TRUE, polygonalpha = 0,
  subjects = as.numeric(chickdata$Chick[!duplicated(ChickWeight$Diet)]))
```

Predicted growth for one chick on each diet, from the diet alone.

## Documentation

- The [website](https://cdriveraus.github.io/ctsem/) has the help pages grouped
  by task, the vignettes and the
  [manual](https://cdriveraus.github.io/ctsem/articles/hierarchicalmanual.pdf).
- A [tutorial paper](https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv/4q9ex_v3) works through
  an applied example, with [code and materials](https://osf.io/xh6ue/).
- Vignettes:
  [getting started](https://cdriveraus.github.io/ctsem/articles/ctsem.html),
  [reading continuous time dynamics](https://cdriveraus.github.io/ctsem/articles/dynamics.html),
  [interventions and time dependent predictors](https://cdriveraus.github.io/ctsem/articles/interventions.html),
  [model syntax](https://cdriveraus.github.io/ctsem/articles/model-syntax.html),
  [measurement models](https://cdriveraus.github.io/ctsem/articles/measurement-models.html),
  [multilevel random effects](https://cdriveraus.github.io/ctsem/articles/laplace-multilevel.html),
  [uncertainty](https://cdriveraus.github.io/ctsem/articles/uncertainty.html),
  [score tests](https://cdriveraus.github.io/ctsem/articles/score-tests.html),
  [IRT items](https://cdriveraus.github.io/ctsem/articles/irt-items.html),
  [ordinal or continuous](https://cdriveraus.github.io/ctsem/articles/ordinal-or-continuous.html),
  [sampling weights](https://cdriveraus.github.io/ctsem/articles/sampling-weights.html).
- Examples on the website:
  [why continuous time](https://cdriveraus.github.io/ctsem/articles/continuous-time.html),
  [a single time series](https://cdriveraus.github.io/ctsem/articles/sunspots.html),
  [Kalman filter and smoother](https://cdriveraus.github.io/ctsem/articles/kalman-filter.html),
  [latent growth curves](https://cdriveraus.github.io/ctsem/articles/growth-curves.html),
  [discrete time models](https://cdriveraus.github.io/ctsem/articles/discrete-time.html),
  [accelerated and multiple group designs](https://cdriveraus.github.io/ctsem/articles/accelerated-designs.html),
  [binary and continuous indicators](https://cdriveraus.github.io/ctsem/articles/binary-data.html),
  [individual differences that come from the model](https://cdriveraus.github.io/ctsem/articles/heterogeneity.html).
- Papers on
  [hierarchical continuous time models](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/324093594_Hierarchical_Bayesian_Continuous_Time_Dynamic_Modeling)
  and on
  [modelling interventions](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/328221807_Understanding_the_Time_Course_of_Interventions_with_Continuous_Time_Dynamic_Models).
- [ctsemGUI](https://github.com/cdriveraus/ctsemgui) is a point-and-click
  interface, and [ctsemOMX](https://github.com/cdriveraus/ctsemOMX) the
  original OpenMx based ctsem.

## Help

Ask questions in [discussions](https://github.com/cdriveraus/ctsem/discussions)
and report bugs as [issues](https://github.com/cdriveraus/ctsem/issues). To cite
ctsem, run `citation('ctsem')`.

<details><summary>Older function names</summary>

Functions renamed in version 3.11 keep their old names as aliases, so older code
still runs.

| old | new |
|---|---|
| `ctStanFit()` | `ctFit()` |
| `ctStanModel()` | `ctModelConvertOMX()` |
| `ctStanGenerate()` | `ctGenerate(fromPriors = TRUE)` |
| `ctStanGenerateFromFit()` | `ctGenerateFromFit()` |
| `ctStanKalman()` | `ctKalmanArray()` |
| `ctStanPlotPost()` | `ctPlotPosterior()` |
| `ctStanPostPredict()` | `ctPostPredPlots()` |
| `ctStanSubjectPars()` | `ctSubjectPars()` |
| `ctStanTIpredeffects()` | `ctTIpredEffects()` |
| `ctStanFitUpdate()` | `ctFitUpdate()` |
| `ctStanDiscretePars()` | `ctDiscretePars()` |
| `ctStanDiscreteParsPlot()` | `ctDiscreteParsPlot()` |
| `ctStanContinuousPars()` | `ctSummaryMatrices()` |
| `ctStanParnames()` | `ctRawParnames()` |

Renames in version 4 are listed in [New in version 4](NEW-IN-4.md).

</details>
